item.title: A trading lab for two
item.description: A friend and I wanted somewhere to try out trading ideas together: European, US and Asian stocks, some crypto, and no real money. Two people, two laptops, one place where the code, the data and the results live. This …
item.content:encoded:
A friend and I wanted somewhere to try out trading ideas together: European, US and Asian stocks, some crypto, and no real money. Two people, two laptops, one place where the code, the data and the results live. This is how that place came together on my homelab, what didn’t work the way we expected, and what we have now.

What we tried first

The lab started with OpenTerminalUI, a terminal for market data. It asked its data providers for prices every five seconds, around the clock, which my DNS filter flagged as suspicious, and it mostly knew Indian and US markets. For two European investors it was the wrong tool, so it went.

What stayed from that start is OpenBB as the data source: one API in front of Yahoo Finance and about 30 other providers. Our notebooks fetch prices from it, and Claude can too, through an MCP connector.

What the lab is made of

  • JupyterLab is the one place we write code, a shared server whose work folder is a Git repository we both push to.
  • NautilusTrader tests ideas on stocks right inside a notebook: fetch prices from OpenBB, define a strategy, see the result under the cell.
  • Freqtrade runs crypto bots around the clock, watched through its web interface, FreqUI. Only with play money: no exchange keys, and the deploy fails if anyone turns paper trading off.
  • TradingAgents lets a few LLM “analysts” debate one stock and give a rating. That one costs real API money, so it has a small monthly limit.
  • Claude in the notebook: JupyterLab’s chat, Jupyter AI, talks to Claude through an OpenAI-compatible gateway on my own subscription (ocp), with a key just for the lab. It explains cells, writes strategies and adds cells to the open notebook.
flowchart LR
  OBB[(OpenBB: prices)] --> NB
  subgraph JL [JupyterLab]
    NB[Notebooks]
    ST[Strategies]
    AI[Claude chat]
  end
  NB --> NT[NautilusTrader: result under the cell]
  ST --> FT[Freqtrade bots]
  FT --> UI[FreqUI]

The starter notebook tests SAP with a simple rule: buy when the 10-day average crosses above the 30-day one, sell when it crosses back.

Everyone signs in with one account on the lab’s own domain; how that works without opening the rest of my homelab is in the sign-in post.

What didn’t work the way we expected

A bot is not what we thought. We expected to open FreqUI, add a bot, pick a strategy and go. In Freqtrade, one running program is one bot, with one config, one strategy and one wallet. FreqUI’s “login to your bot” window doesn’t create anything; it saves a connection to a bot that already runs, and it saves it in the browser. And a bot that trades can’t backtest: that needs a second Freqtrade in another mode.

The last step needed me. Moving a tested strategy onto the running bot meant copying a file and restarting a container, so my friend would have had to ask me for the most interesting part of the whole lab.

What we have now

Two bots, and one folder for each:

  • Backtest sits idle until you pick a strategy in FreqUI and click start; then it replays past prices in about a minute. Its folder, backtest/, holds every experiment.
  • Paper-Trading runs one strategy all day with play money. Its folder, paper-trading/, holds only what runs.
flowchart LR
  T[Template strategy] -->|duplicate| E[Your strategy in backtest/]
  E --> BB[Backtest bot: past prices, on click]
  BB -->|good enough| TO[Notebook: take it over]
  TO --> PB[Paper-Trading bot: live prices, play money]
  BB --> UI[FreqUI]
  PB --> UI

The workflow:

  1. In backtest/, duplicate the template strategy and rename it.

  2. Change it and test it in the Backtest bot. Freqtrade’s example strategy over the last month made 24 trades and turned 10,000 into 7,551 USDT of play money. It’s an example, not a suggestion.

  3. When it’s good, take it over yourself: a notebook lists the strategies, you write one file name and press run. It has the Backtest bot load the strategy for real first, so a broken one is refused before anything changes. Then it copies it in, reloads the Paper-Trading bot and waits until it runs again. If it doesn’t come back, the previous strategy is put back.

FreqUI opens with both bots already there, because a small start page fills in what FreqUI would otherwise ask for. JupyterLab opens on the repository’s README, with a diagram of which folder belongs to which tool, and every folder has its own README. The lab’s wiki has one page per workflow plus a page of links for learning Python and Jupyter.

What I took from it

  • Learn the tool’s model before naming things. Our folders are named after the bots now, because a strategy belongs to one bot.
  • If someone has to ask you to do a step, that step isn’t finished.
  • No real money until it’s a separate, deliberate decision. Everything here is backtests and paper trading, and the setup makes sure it stays that way.

item.title: Letting people outside the household into my homelab
item.description: Until this month, everyone with an account on my homelab lived in our flat. That made a lot of things easy without my noticing. Then a friend and I started a trading lab together, and my dad may get a cloud folder …
item.content:encoded:
Until this month, everyone with an account on my homelab lived in our flat. That made a lot of things easy without my noticing. Then a friend and I started a trading lab together, and my dad may get a cloud folder later. Neither of them should see the rest of the homelab, and neither should see the household’s own domain at all. This post is about what that took on the sign-in side.

Accounts that opened everything

Every app sits behind Authentik, reached through Caddy. Authentik has one default that only matters once there are strangers: an application without a policy binding is open to every signed-in user.

When I counted, 39 of my 43 applications had no binding. An account for my friend would have opened Home Assistant, the cameras, the photos, the documents, Proxmox and Grafana. Nobody had noticed, because the only accounts were the two of us.

The fix is boring on purpose:

  • Every application is bound to a group: the household apps to the household group, the trading apps to a trading group, later the cloud folder to a group just for my dad.
  • Who is in which group lives in one file in git, next to the bindings.
  • The deploy fails when an application has no binding. A new app can’t be open by accident; someone has to decide who gets in.

I ran an access matrix before and after: every user against every application. The two household accounts got the same answers as before on all 43 apps. A test user in no group was refused everywhere.

A second front door

Outsiders get their own domain, marceltov.de, with its own sign-in page at auth.marceltov.de. It is still one Authentik, with a second brand: its own title, its own password-reset flow, and mails from an address on that domain. I tested the reset end to end with a throwaway user: the mail landed in the inbox, not in spam, and the link pointed to the right domain.

The surprise was the outpost, the part of Authentik that checks every request Caddy hands it. Authentik’s built-in outpost always sends the browser to the sign-in domain it was set up with, whichever domain the app is on. So an app on marceltov.de sent outsiders to the household’s login page. The way out was a second, standalone outpost just for marceltov.de, which can be told where to send the browser. It is one more small container.

flowchart LR
  B[Browser] --> CF[Cloudflare] --> C[Caddy]
  C -->|household domain| O1[Built-in outpost]
  C -->|marceltov.de| O2[Standalone outpost]
  O1 --> A[(One Authentik)]
  O2 --> A
  A -->|group bound to the app?| APP[App]
  A -.->|no binding: deploy fails| X[Refused]

In the Raspberry Pi post I wondered whether to swap Authentik for the lighter Authelia. Brands, groups and outposts are exactly what this needed, so Authentik stays.

Apps that bring their own login

Not every app is happy behind a proxy, and a second login on top of the first helps nobody:

  • Wiki.js signs in with OpenID Connect and maps Authentik’s groups onto its own, so each group sees only its own pages.
  • FreqUI, the trading bot’s web interface, has one shared password and its own login window. Caddy now fills that password in after Authentik has let you through, so nobody types it. The trading post has the details.
  • MCP servers are what Claude connects to from claude.ai, and those connectors sign in with OAuth, which most servers don’t do themselves. The OAuth front I built for Trilium, trilium-mcp-proxy, has grown into mcp-login-proxy (GitHub): one front for any MCP server, with the same Authentik account behind it. OpenBB, Grafana and OpenCloud sit behind it now. For OpenCloud it also fixed an annoyance: its old connector asked for a new sign-in every hour, because its token had no way to refresh.

Docs that outsiders can read

The internal documentation stays where it is. People outside the household get a separate wiki, wiki.marceltov.de, with usage docs only: how to sign in and how to do things, no hostnames, no addresses. Each task is one page with one diagram and its steps.

One thing needed fixing there: Wiki.js 3.5 recognises Mermaid diagrams but doesn’t draw them on pages. A short script in the theme settings does now.

What I took from it

  • A default that’s harmless with two users becomes a hole with three. Make it a rule the deploy checks, not something to remember.
  • Test with the people you are protecting against: a user in no group, a mail to a real inbox.
  • Write the docs for the reader. My friend doesn’t need to know where things run; he needs to know what to click.

item.title: Neues Modell: Schneeflocken-Dose für eine SD-Karte
item.description: Ursprünglich wollten wir einfach eine SD-Karte verschenken. Daraus ist diese kleine Schneeflocken-Dose geworden: eine Dose, die sich mit einer Vierteldrehung öffnen und schließen lässt.
item.content:encoded:
Ursprünglich wollten wir einfach eine SD-Karte verschenken. Daraus ist diese kleine Schneeflocken-Dose geworden: eine Dose, die sich mit einer Vierteldrehung öffnen und schließen lässt.

Deckel aufsetzen, 60 Grad drehen, fertig. Das Schöne daran: 60 Grad sind genau der Abstand von einem Arm zum nächsten, also stehen die sechs Arme nach dem Schließen immer perfekt deckungsgleich. Keine schiefe Schneeflocke, nie. Ein kleiner Rasthöcker hält den Deckel zu, bis man ihn wieder aufdreht.

Die Dose besteht aus zwei Hälften mit einem Bajonett-Verschluss und wird komplett ohne Stützen gedruckt. Die Arme bleiben schön spitz, nur die oberen und unteren Kanten sind sanft abgerundet, damit nichts in die Finger schneidet.

Für die SD-Karte gibt es einen optionalen Einsatz, der sie sauber an ihrem Platz hält, damit sie in der Dose nicht herumrutscht.

So wird aus einer einzelnen SD-Karte ein richtiges kleines Geschenk.

Wer keinen Einsatz braucht, nutzt die Dose einfach als kleine Schmuck- oder Krimskrams-Dose: für einen Ring, eine Münze, Kopfhörer oder was auch immer hineinpasst.

Und das Beste: Das Modell ist komplett parametrisch. Über den MakerWorld-Customizer lassen sich Innendurchmesser und Höhe selbst einstellen, ganz ohne ein einziges Programm zu installieren. Flach für eine Karte, tiefer für kleine Schätze, ganz wie man möchte.

Für den festlichen Look haben wir sie auf einer strukturierten Druckplatte mit Sternen-Muster gedruckt, das sorgt für eine fein glitzernde Unterseite. Und als oberes und unteres Flächenmuster haben wir Octagram Spiral gewählt, das sich zu einem kleinen Stern dreht und perfekt zur Schneeflocke passt.

Kostenlos und anpassbar auf MakerWorld: hier geht’s zum Modell. Frohes Drucken und eine schöne Weihnachtszeit.

item.title: Moving my homelab's monitoring onto a Raspberry Pi, and making it fit
item.description: Until mid-November, everything that watches my homelab ran on the homelab itself. DNS (AdGuard), the reverse proxy (Caddy), sign-in (Authentik) and the whole monitoring stack (Grafana, Prometheus, InfluxDB, Loki) …
item.content:encoded:
Until mid-November, everything that watches my homelab ran on the homelab itself. DNS (AdGuard), the reverse proxy (Caddy), sign-in (Authentik) and the whole monitoring stack (Grafana, Prometheus, InfluxDB, Loki) were containers on my one Proxmox server, a Beelink mini PC that runs every service we use.

Why it moved

When the Beelink went down once, it took everything with it at the same moment. DNS stopped for the whole flat, nothing could send an alert, and there was nothing to open to see what had happened before it died.

So the goal became: when the server dies, a phone alert still arrives, DNS keeps working, and Grafana and the logs can be opened from home or away, while the server is still down. For that, all of it has to live on a machine that isn’t the server. That machine is a Raspberry Pi 4 with 4 GB of RAM and an SSD, which I call monitor-pi.

  • What moved: AdGuard, Caddy, Authentik, CrowdSec, Grafana, Gatus (uptime checks), and the stores for every metric and log the homelab produces, with their history.
  • Caddy and Authentik had to move too. Reaching Grafana from outside while the server is dead needs the proxy and the sign-in off the server as well.
  • Measured beforehand: AdGuard, Grafana and the stores used about 1.3 GiB on the server, against 3.6 GiB available on the Pi. It fit on paper.
  • Moved on 2026-11-16.

It didn’t fit

The first day looked fine: swap reads on the Pi were around 30 pages per second. After its first restart, they jumped to around 1,900 pages per second and stayed there. Every program kept pulling its memory back from the SSD, and DNS and everything behind the proxy got slower.

Two things made it worse than the estimate:

  • Caddy, Authentik and CrowdSec weren’t in the 1.3 GiB. Authentik alone (server, worker and its Postgres) holds about 800 MiB.
  • On the server nobody had looked at how much RAM this stack costs: with 28 GB, it never mattered. On the Pi it was the whole budget.

Why the first day fit and the restart didn’t is still unknown.

The goal

“No frequent swapping, only if there is extensive workload running there.” Written down so it can be checked: swap reads below 50 pages/s in at least 95 % of the hours of a normal week.

How full swap is doesn’t matter. Swap still holds about 1.5 GiB today. What costs time is reading it back. So I measured the read rate (pswpin), and how much time programs actually stall waiting for memory (PSI).

Step 0: measure before changing anything

  • PSI (Pressure Stall Information) on. Raspberry Pi kernels ship it off, so it took a kernel flag and one reboot.
  • Per-container swap reads every minute, from each container’s cgroup (workingset_refault_anon), because the host’s counter doesn’t say who is reading back.

There was no single culprit; the whole box was short. Grafana, InfluxDB, Prometheus and Authentik led the ranking. AdGuard was surprisingly high too: its memory reservation turned out to be best-effort only, so the kernel swapped it out as well.

The path

What replaced what

The collector was picked by a trial on the same host (median memory): Fluent Bit 15 MiB, Vector 46 MiB, Alloy 97 MiB.

Nothing had to be torn up for the switch:

  • VictoriaMetrics scrapes the same targets Prometheus did, and accepts InfluxDB’s line protocol. Every Proxmox host, backup server and script kept its own write-only token, now checked by vmauth.
  • 33 alert queries and 100 dashboard queries were rewritten from Flux to MetricsQL. Each one was compared against the original on the same data before the switch.
  • One VictoriaLogs datasource replaced 25 Loki ones.
  • The old data stays on the Pi for 30 days in case I need to roll back.

The trend so far

Every hour since the switch has been under the goal (median 20, max 28 pages/s, 11 hours so far). Memory PSI went from 6–18 % to at most 0.2 %. Still, these were night hours. The verdict comes after a full week, on 2026-11-27.

What went wrong on the way

  • Grafana crash-looped for about 3 minutes. Renaming a provisioned datasource while keeping its id is refused.
  • The Beelink’s logs were dropped for about 7 minutes. VictoriaLogs reads Loki’s tenant header as a number and answered “400” to a name.
  • 14 of 18 hosts’ container logs were missing for about 3 hours. Their Docker logs to the journal, not to files. Only 4 hosts showed up right after the rollout, and we put it down to a quiet night instead of checking. Fixed, and the gap was refilled.
  • A JSON import answered 200 and stored nothing. It was missing one Content-Type header.
  • The nightly backup failed once on a leftover step from the day before. It was rerun and verified.
  • And one good find: an “offsite backup stale” alert had been false all day. The old Flux query silently ignored half of the runs.

Lesson: after switching a pipeline, count the rows and the hosts that arrive. A 200 isn’t proof.

Next

  • 2026-11-27: the week’s verdict, then a tighter swap alert.
  • Maybe Grafana itself (~650 MiB) → vmalert + Alertmanager + Perses (~60 MiB). Only if the week says it’s needed.
  • Maybe Authentik → Authelia: lighter, and configured from one file.

item.title: "Too much RF interference" that wasn't
item.description: I updated the firmware of our Zigbee coordinator (an SMLIGHT SLZB-06P7) this morning, after taking a ZHA backup. Afterwards Home Assistant could not bring the network back. Every restore failed with:
item.content:encoded:
I updated the firmware of our Zigbee coordinator (an SMLIGHT SLZB-06P7) this morning, after taking a ZHA backup. Afterwards Home Assistant could not bring the network back. Every restore failed with:

zigpy.exceptions.FormationFailure: Network formation refused: there is too much RF interference. Make sure your coordinator is on a USB 2.0 extension cable and away from any sources of interference, like USB 3.0 ports, SSDs, 2.4GHz routers, motherboards, etc.

So I went hunting for interference. Three more firmware builds, power cycles, an energy scan. Nothing changed, and our flat had no Zigbee for 77 minutes.

What actually happened

The message was wrong about the cause.

  1. Flashing the radio erases the network it holds. PAN ID, network key, frame counters: gone. Only the backup in Home Assistant still has them.
  2. Restoring the backup is a network formation. Before the flash the radio just resumed its stored network; now it has to form it again, and before forming it scans the channel.
  3. The scan finds the network already running. Every Zigbee plug and lamp in the flat is a router, and they all kept the old network alive during the flash. The radio sees its own PAN ID on the air, refuses to form it, and zigpy-znp reports the timeout as “too much RF interference”.

The fix: ten seconds with a screwdriver

Unscrew the coordinator’s antenna so it cannot hear the routers, run the restore, screw the antenna back on. The network came back, and not a single device had to be re-paired. The next firmware update, done that way from the start, restored itself in 90 seconds.

If you flash a Zigbee coordinator

  • Take a backup first.
  • Make the coordinator deaf to your routers (antenna off, or switch off the routers near it).
  • Flash, restore, then reconnect the antenna.
  • If you see “too much RF interference” right after a flash, think “my own network is still on the air” before you think “interference”.

SMLIGHT’s manual actually says it: the same message appears when a network with the same PAN ID already exists. I found that page an hour too late.

item.title: Running Home Assistant with Claude, and making sure nothing gets lost
item.description: My 3D printer draws 16 watts doing nothing. On 18 November it did that for three hours and 23 minutes after the print was done, because nobody walked over to switch it off:
item.content:encoded:
My 3D printer draws 16 watts doing nothing. On 18 November it did that for three hours and 23 minutes after the print was done, because nobody walked over to switch it off:

So I asked Claude, in one sentence, to switch the printer’s plug off ten minutes after a print finishes. A minute later the automation existed in my Home Assistant. This post is about what happened in that minute, why I trust it, and what I built around it so that nothing gets lost and I notice when something breaks. At the end there is a tutorial if you want the same.

One sentence, one automation

Claude talks to my Home Assistant through ha-mcp, an MCP server that runs as an integration inside Home Assistant itself, installed through HACS. Claude sends a request, ha-mcp turns it into Home Assistant’s own API calls.

For the printer, Claude searched my entities, found the printer’s status sensor (finish when a print is done) and the plug, and wrote this (entity names simplified):

triggers:
  - trigger: state
    entity_id: sensor.druckstatus
    to: finish
    for: { minutes: 10 }
    not_from: [unavailable, unknown, offline]
conditions:
  - condition: state
    entity_id: switch.3d_drucker
    state: "on"
actions:
  - action: switch.turn_off
    target: { entity_id: switch.3d_drucker }

The detail I like most is something I did not ask for. ha-mcp ships a best-practices guide for Home Assistant, and in its strict mode it refuses any write until the guide has been read: the guide contains a key that changes every hour, and a write without the current key is rejected. So Claude cannot “just quickly” write an automation the way it half-remembers from 2023; it has to read how Home Assistant wants it done today first.

It still was not perfect on the first try, and the line not_from is the proof. The first version had only to: finish. That evening Home Assistant restarted, the printer’s status came back from unavailable to finish, and to the automation that looked like a print that had just ended. It would have switched off a printer nobody had touched. Switching the printer on does the same, because it reports its last status (finish) after being offline. Claude found this in the history the same evening, and the fix is one line. I mention it because it is the honest picture: the assistant is fast and careful, and a change that goes live immediately still needs a safety net.

Nothing gets lost

There are two different things that can go wrong, and they need two different answers.

The machine dies. Home Assistant runs as a virtual machine, and every night its whole disk is backed up; a second machine keeps a copy, and a third copy goes offsite. That restores everything, but it cannot tell me what changed.

An automation breaks, or a change was a mistake. For that I want history: a diff, with a date. So once a day a small job copies Home Assistant’s YAML into a private git repository and commits when something changed.

The copy is an allowlist: configuration.yaml, automations.yaml, scripts.yaml, scenes.yaml, packages/, blueprints/ and the ESPHome device files. Never secrets.yaml, never .storage/.

The first snapshot still pushed two secrets. A login secret for one integration had been written straight into configuration.yaml, and an ESPHome device had its API key inline. Neither file was on any deny-list, because the problem was not the file, it was a line in it. The repo was private, I deleted and recreated it anyway, and since then the job refuses to push in three cases:

  1. The copy is empty. A moved or empty /config would otherwise “delete” my whole config in git.
  2. A value sits under a key named like a credential (password, token, key, …) and is not !secret, a template or empty; or there is a Bearer header or a URL with a password in it.
  3. Any value from secrets.yaml appears anywhere in the copy, under whatever key. This one I added on 18 November, and I took the idea from someone else.

Why I did not use Git Exporter

There is a Home Assistant app (formerly add-on) called Git Exporter that does roughly what my job does, installed with a few clicks. I read its code before switching to it. Its secret check is better than my first one: it turns every value in secrets.yaml into a search pattern, which is exactly check 3 above. Everything else made me stay: its last release was in 2024, it reports error on every run where nothing changed (so a real failure looks like a quiet day), and it can only push with a personal access token tied to my account. So I borrowed the idea and left the app.

How I notice

A backup nobody checks and an automation nobody watches are hopes, not systems. Home Assistant has a built-in Prometheus export; my Prometheus reads it every minute and Grafana turns it into a dashboard and four alerts that reach my phone through ntfy:

  • Home Assistant does not answer for 5 minutes.
  • A battery is below 20 %, one message per device.
  • A battery device has been unavailable for 24 hours. A dead Zigbee sensor rarely reports 0 %; it just disappears.
  • No successful config snapshot in 26 hours.

The battery alerts carry a label that holds them between 22:00 and 07:00. Nothing about a battery needs to wake anyone up; they arrive with the morning coffee instead.

There turned out to be a lot to watch:

And the first look at the batteries was a to-do list: four devices under 20 %, one at zero.

The dashboard also lists every entity Home Assistant currently calls unavailable. On the first evening that was 529 of them: leftovers of removed devices, integrations that lost their login, things that are simply switched off. That is not an alert, it is a list I sweep through now and then.

Tutorial: the same for your Home Assistant

You need a Home Assistant OS or Supervised install (for apps), a GitHub account, and a Linux machine that is always on (a Raspberry Pi is fine).

1. Let Claude manage Home Assistant

  1. Install HACS if you do not have it.
  2. In HACS, download the integration HA-MCP (homeassistant-ai/ha-mcp), restart Home Assistant, then add it under Settings → Devices & services.
  3. Connect your Claude client to it as described in the project’s README. Reach Home Assistant over HTTPS only.
  4. Turn on its strict best-practices mode if your version offers it as an option, and ask Claude for something small first. Read what it wrote in the automation editor.

Changes go live immediately. Do steps 2 and 3 before you let it change anything important.

2. Put your config into git, safely

In Home Assistant, install the Terminal & SSH app. In its configuration, add your Linux machine’s public SSH key to authorized_keys, add rsync to its packages, and map port 22 in its network settings.

On GitHub, create a private repository and add a deploy key with write access (a separate SSH key that can push to this one repository and nothing else). Clone it on your Linux machine.

Save this as /usr/local/bin/ha-git-snapshot.sh and set HA and REPO at the top:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Copy Home Assistant's YAML into a git repo once a day, refuse anything that
# looks like a secret, commit only when something changed, push.
set -euo pipefail
HA=root@homeassistant.local      # your Home Assistant
REPO=$HOME/homeassistant-config  # a clone of your private repo

cd "$REPO"
git pull -q --ff-only || true

# 1. The allowlist: your hand-written YAML, never secrets.yaml or .storage/.
rsync -a -m --delete --exclude=.git/ --exclude=README.md \
  --exclude=secrets.yaml --exclude=.storage/ --exclude='/esphome/.*' \
  --include=/configuration.yaml --include=/automations.yaml \
  --include=/scripts.yaml --include=/scenes.yaml \
  --include='/packages/***' --include='/blueprints/***' \
  --include=/esphome/ --include='/esphome/*.yaml' \
  --exclude='*' "$HA:/config/" ./
[ -f configuration.yaml ] || { echo "empty copy, refusing"; exit 1; }

# 2. A password written inline instead of through !secret.
if grep -rnEi --include='*.yaml' \
     '(password|token|api_key|secret):[[:space:]]+[^[:space:]!{"'"'"']' . ; then
  echo "inline secret above: move it to secrets.yaml and use !secret"; exit 1
fi

# 3. A value from secrets.yaml that shows up anywhere (whatever the key).
SECRETS=$(mktemp); trap 'rm -f "$SECRETS"' EXIT
ssh "$HA" cat /config/secrets.yaml 2>/dev/null \
  | sed -nE 's/^[^#:]+:[[:space:]]*"?([^"#]*[^"#[:space:]])"?.*$/\1/p' \
  | awk 'length >= 8' > "$SECRETS"
if [ -s "$SECRETS" ] && grep -rlF -f "$SECRETS" --exclude-dir=.git . ; then
  echo "a value from secrets.yaml is in the files above"; exit 1
fi

# 4. Commit and push only when something changed.
git add -A
git diff --cached --quiet || { git commit -qm "snapshot $(date +%F)"; git push -q; }
echo ok

Run it once by hand and look at what landed on GitHub: no secrets.yaml, no .storage. Then let cron run it daily:

0 4 * * * /usr/local/bin/ha-git-snapshot.sh >> /var/log/ha-git-snapshot.log 2>&1

I ran exactly this script against my own Home Assistant (into a local test repository) before publishing it, and fed both checks a planted password and a planted secret value: both refused. It is a simpler sibling of what I run myself, which adds tests, a staging copy that is checked before it touches the repo, and an alert when it has not succeeded for a day.

3. Watch it from Grafana

If you already have Prometheus and Grafana:

  1. Add this to configuration.yaml and restart Home Assistant: 
    prometheus:
  namespace: homeassistant
  2. Create a separate user for Prometheus (Settings → People, not an administrator, local network only), log in as that user once, and create a long-lived access token under Profile → Security. Be aware it is not read-only: Home Assistant has no read-only users, a non-admin can still switch devices. Keep the token like a password.
  3. Scrape it: 
    - job_name: homeassistant
  scrape_interval: 60s
  metrics_path: /api/prometheus
  authorization:
    credentials_file: /etc/prometheus/secrets/homeassistant-token
  static_configs:
    - targets: ['homeassistant.local:8123']
  4. In Grafana, alert on up{job="homeassistant"} below 1 for 5 minutes, and on homeassistant_sensor_battery_percent below 20 for 30 minutes. Leave out your phones and tablets with a label matcher such as entity!~"sensor[.](https://notefeed.me/r/marcelbruckner/my_phone|my_tablet).*": they cross 20 % every day.

One thing that cost me a deploy: write sensor[.] and not sensor\. in PromQL. Prometheus uses Go string escaping and rejects \..

What I would tell someone starting today

  • Let the assistant do the typing, and keep the safety net yourself: a nightly backup for disasters, git for history, alerts for silence.
  • Check what your history pushes. My allowlist was right and still leaked, because the secret was in a line, not a file.
  • Before installing the convenient tool, read its code. Sometimes you keep the idea and leave the tool.
  • Alert on batteries, but not at night.
