item.content:encoded:
Ab heute kannst du zuschauen, während mein Drucker arbeitet. Auf der Seite Drucker siehst du ein Bild aus meiner Druckecke, das sich etwa alle zehn Sekunden erneuert. Auf der Startseite ersetzt es während eines Drucks das Foto vom Drucker.

Was du siehst

Ein Standbild, kein Video. Darunter steht, wie weit der Druck ist und wann er ungefähr fertig wird. Läuft gerade nichts, steht dort „Gerade läuft kein Druck“.

Was du nicht siehst

Die Kamera schaut auf den Drucker. Das Regal daneben schneidet sie schon selbst ab, bevor das Bild entsteht. Das Bild gibt es nur, solange ein Druck läuft. Was gedruckt wird und für wen, steht nirgends: Datei- und Auftragsnamen bleiben bei mir.

Soll ein Druck nicht zu sehen sein, schalte ich das Bild mit einem Tipp ab. Nach dem Druck ist es von selbst wieder an. Wenn du bei mir bestellst und das lieber nicht öffentlich hättest, sag einfach Bescheid.

Wie es funktioniert

Es ist dieselbe Kamera, die schon auf „Spaghetti“ aufpasst. Während eines Drucks schickt ein kleines Programm bei mir zu Hause alle zehn Sekunden das neueste Bild an meinen Server bei Hetzner, und von dort bekommst du es. Dein Browser fragt also nie bei mir zu Hause an. Hört das Programm auf zu schicken, verschwindet das Bild nach einer halben Minute. Gespeichert wird immer nur das neueste Bild, und auch das nur im Arbeitsspeicher.

item.title: Auditing a self-hosted finance app before it meets my bank
item.description: I wanted one place that shows all my money: current accounts, savings, depots, loans. I did not want that place to be someone else's cloud. So I set up Securo, an open-source finance manager, on my own server, and …
item.content:encoded:
I wanted one place that shows all my money: current accounts, savings, depots, loans. I did not want that place to be someone else’s cloud. So I set up Securo, an open-source finance manager, on my own server, and before I let it near a bank account I had Claude read its code with me. This is what came out of that day, in the order it happened.

Reading the code first

Securo is eight months old, mostly written by one person, and ships a release every few days. That is no reason to avoid it, but it is a reason to look.

We read the parts that decide who gets in and what they can see: sign-in, API tokens, how data is separated between workspaces, the bank connection, file storage, and every endpoint that works without a login. Both dependency lockfiles went through the OSV vulnerability database. Then we probed my running instance from outside.

What held up:

  • 26 of 329 API operations work without a login, and with local passwords switched off the sensitive ones answer 403.
  • Single sign-on is done properly (PKCE, nonce, issuer and audience checked).
  • No raw SQL, no path tricks in file storage, API tokens are hashed and scoped.
  • No telemetry. The server only talks to the providers you configure.

What did not:

  • The session token lives in the browser’s localStorage, is valid for 24 hours, and logging out does not revoke it.
  • The app sends no security headers.
  • The bank connection’s credentials sit unencrypted in the database, next to a code comment that says “Encrypted tokens”.
  • The interactive API documentation is public.

None of that is a hole by itself. Together it means one injected script would be enough to take over a session.

A policy the app does not send

The fix did not need a change to Securo. My reverse proxy (Caddy) now adds a Content-Security-Policy in front of it: scripts only from the site itself, requests only to the site and to GitHub’s release check. An injected script can no longer run, and could not send the token anywhere if it did.

You can write such a policy without clicking through the app. Fetch the built index.html; if it has no inline script, script-src 'self' works. Then grep the frontend source for what it loads from elsewhere (fonts, logos, blob: previews, a PDF worker) and allow exactly that. The proxy also answers 404 for the API documentation.

What “connect your bank” really gives you

Securo talks to European banks through Enable Banking, a Finnish provider that is licensed only to read account information. That limit is the good news: whatever goes wrong, nobody can move money through it. For your own accounts it is free.

Three things I did not expect:

  1. You approve twice. First you link your accounts in Enable Banking’s control panel, which only puts them on your application’s allow-list. Then the app asks for its own consent, and the bank has you approve again.
  2. You get 90 days of history, not years.
  3. You get current accounts and nothing else. The law behind this interface (PSD2) covers payment accounts. Savings accounts, depots and loans are not offered through it, whichever aggregator you pick. One of my banks delivers transactions with amount and date only, no text at all.

The part that takes weeks

For savings accounts and depots, German banks have their own older protocol, FinTS. It logs in as you, with your online-banking PIN, which is a very different kind of trust than a read-only consent. And every program that speaks it, a private script included, needs a registration number from the banking association: a PDF form, sent by e-mail, answered in “two weeks or longer”.

Put together, this is how each kind of account gets into the app:

I sent the form. Until the number arrives, the depots go in by hand.

What I would tell someone starting today

  • Read the code of anything that gets your bank data, or have it read. It took an afternoon.
  • Put the security headers in your proxy if the app does not send them.
  • Decide what you want to see before you connect anything. I imported a year of CSV first, then connected the bank, and had the last 90 days twice.
  • Expect “bank sync” to mean current accounts. Everything else is still work.

item.title: Rescuing a dying USB stick: recovering truncated files with rsync, photorec & tag-matching
item.description: I just rescued a dying USB music stick, and the failure mode is sneaky enough to be worth writing up: a failing FAT flash drive can lie to every copy tool. The directory still lists each file at its original size, …
item.content:encoded:
I just rescued a dying USB music stick, and the failure mode is sneaky enough to be worth writing up: a failing FAT flash drive can lie to every copy tool. The directory still lists each file at its original size, but the filesystem can only hand back the first cluster or two. cp, Finder, even rsync all report success while silently truncating your files. Here’s the full runbook (macOS, but the tools are cross-platform).

The symptom that fools you

A flash drive (USB stick, SD card) is dying but not dead. Files are all listed, yet some won’t open — and a normal copy produces files that play for a second and cut off. The dead giveaway: every damaged file ends on an exact multiple of the cluster size (32768 B = 32 KB on mine).

That’s lost FAT cluster chains. FAT stores a file as a linked chain of clusters; when the link bytes rot, the filesystem follows the chain only to the break and stops — but the directory entry still carries the full size, so tools think the copy is complete. A 4-minute MP3 that’s only 32 KB has its header intact (players show full duration) but almost no audio. The tail data usually still sits physically on the flash, reachable only by reading raw sectors.

1. Salvage what’s still readable (no root)

rsync -rt --partial --no-perms --no-owner --no-group \
  --exclude='._*' --exclude='.Spotlight-V100' --exclude='.fseventsd' \
  "/Volumes/NAME/" dest/

--partial keeps half-read files; rsync skips unreadable ones and exits 23 (“partial transfer”). Compare file count and total bytes, source vs dest.

2. Find the silent truncation

Don’t trust the copy — decode-test every file. Anything that errors, or whose size ÷ duration implies an absurd bitrate (< ~40 kbps), is truncated:

ffmpeg -v error -i FILE -f null -     # any output = problem
ffprobe -v error -show_entries format=duration -of csv=p=0 FILE

Confirm with the round-block test: size % 32768 == 0 on the damaged files = cluster-chain loss, not a genuinely small file.

3. Carve the raw flash (needs root)

PhotoRec ignores the filesystem and rebuilds files from their content signatures across the whole device, including free space and orphaned clusters:

brew install testdisk
sudo photorec /log /d OUT/recup /cmd /dev/rdiskN \
  fileopt,everything,disable,mp3,enable,mov,enable,search
  • Use the raw node /dev/rdiskN (faster), find it with diskutil list.
  • mov covers mp4/m4a/3gp; add whatever signatures you need.
  • If the drive stalls on bad sectors, image it first with ddrescue (resumable, gentle) and carve the image instead of hammering the dying device.

4. Rename & re-match the carved files

Carved files come out as fNNNNNNNN.mp3 with no names — but ID3/MP4 tags usually survive. Read artist/title/duration with ffprobe, fuzzy-match (normalised token overlap) back to your truncated originals, keep the largest non-truncated copy per track, and decode-test before trusting it. Bare filenames (11 Represent.mp3) need title-only matching; pin ambiguous ones (Intro, Outro) to the known album artist.

Gotchas

  1. rsync reports truncated files as copied — always decode-test; never trust the byte count alone.
  2. wholedisk is NOT a valid token in photorec 7.2 — it throws a syntax error; the raw device already is the whole disk.
  3. macOS ._* AppleDouble files and embedded cover art (JPEG mislabelled as PNG) trip ffmpeg -v error — ignore them.
  4. Verdict: a dying stick only gets worse. The moment you’ve salvaged it, stop using it — copy to fresh media and retire it. Every extra read risks more decay.

The result

16 GB FAT32 stick, 32 KB clusters, ~879 files. Decode test found 1 dead, 11 unopenable, 181 truncated to cluster boundaries. PhotoRec carved 818 full files from the raw flash; tag-matching healed 179 of 193. Final library: 6.2 GB — bigger than the 4.2 GB the failing filesystem could even show. Then straight onto a fresh SD card, and retire the old stick for good.

item.title: Mein Drucker hat jetzt ein Auge drauf
item.description: Ein 3D-Druck dauert oft viele Stunden, und ich sitze nicht die ganze Zeit daneben. Meistens geht alles gut. Aber manchmal löst sich ein Teil vom Druckbett, und der Drucker legt sein Filament danach einfach in die …
item.content:encoded:
Ein 3D-Druck dauert oft viele Stunden, und ich sitze nicht die ganze Zeit daneben. Meistens geht alles gut. Aber manchmal löst sich ein Teil vom Druckbett, und der Drucker legt sein Filament danach einfach in die Luft. Heraus kommt ein Knäuel, das Drucker-Leute „Spaghetti“ nennen. Das kostet Material, Zeit und im schlimmsten Fall die Düse.

Deshalb hat mein Drucker jetzt eine Kamera und eine Erkennung, die bei so einem Knäuel Bescheid sagt.

Die Kamera

Neben dem Drucker sitzt ein kleiner Raspberry Pi mit einer Nachtsicht-Kamera. Er filmt das Druckbett und schickt das Bild an meinen Server, der es aufzeichnet. In jedem Bild stehen Datum und Uhrzeit, so sehe ich bei jedem Druck genau, wann was passiert ist.

Die Kamera hängt am selben Stecker wie der Drucker. Ist der Drucker aus, ist auch die Kamera aus. So läuft nichts unnötig, und ich sehe am Stecker, was beide zusammen verbrauchen.

Selbst konstruiert und gedruckt

Das Gehäuse der Kamera habe ich selbst konstruiert und auf genau diesem Drucker gedruckt. Genauso die Halter, mit denen Kamera und Raspberry Pi an der Lochwand hängen. Nur die schwarzen Teile, das Gelenk und die Rändelschrauben, sind Original-Zubehör von GoPro. Meine gedruckten Teile haben dieselben Anschlüsse wie GoPro-Halterungen, deshalb passt beides zusammen, und die Kamera lässt sich in jede Richtung drehen und neigen.

Die Spaghetti-Erkennung

Alle 10 Sekunden schaut sich ein Programm das aktuelle Bild an. Dahinter steckt ein frei verfügbares Erkennungsmodell des Projekts Obico, das genau dafür trainiert wurde: misslungene Drucke zu erkennen. Es läuft komplett bei mir zu Hause, kein Bild verlässt das Haus.

Ein einzelnes verdächtiges Bild löst noch nichts aus. Erst wenn die Erkennung über mehrere Bilder hinweg sicher ist, bekomme ich eine Nachricht aufs Handy, mit einem Foto vom Druckbett. Dann entscheide ich: Ist es wirklich Spaghetti, stoppe ich den Druck. Ist es ein Fehlalarm, tippe ich auf „Fehlalarm“, und der Druck läuft weiter. Reagiere ich nicht, erinnert mich das Handy nach ein paar Minuten noch einmal.

Warum stoppt das nicht von selbst?

Das war die erste Idee. Aber mein Drucker nimmt einen Pause-Befehl nur von der App des Herstellers an. Die einzige Alternative wäre, ihm einfach den Strom abzudrehen. Das ist keine Pause: Der Druck ist verloren, und die heiße Düse verliert schlagartig ihre Kühlung, was sie verstopfen kann. Ein Fehlalarm würde dann einen guten Druck kaputt machen. Darum entscheidet am Ende ein Mensch, und der bin ich.

Was du davon hast

Geht bei deinem Druck etwas schief, merke ich es früh und nicht erst am nächsten Morgen. Ich drucke neu, statt Stunden an einem Knäuel weiterzudrucken, und du bekommst dein Teil schneller. Die Erkennung ist noch neu, ich schaue mir in den nächsten Wochen an, wie oft sie richtig liegt, und stelle sie dann feiner ein.

Fragen zu deinem Druck? Schreib mir an kontakt@3dbruckner.de.

item.title: The RFID rabbit hole: why my door fob wouldn't copy
item.description: I inherited an apartment from the previous renter, and with it a little pile of blue key fobs that open the building door. I wanted more of them. How hard can copying a key fob be? Famous last words. What followed …
item.content:encoded:
The setup that started it all: a spare Raspberry Pi and an RC522 reader. Looks right for the job. Isn’t.

I inherited an apartment from the previous renter, and with it a little pile of blue key fobs that open the building door. I wanted more of them. How hard can copying a key fob be? Famous last words. What followed was an afternoon of debugging that ended with me learning more about RFID than I ever meant to — and ordering a €23 gadget to do what I’d confidently assumed a Raspberry Pi could.

Here’s the whole detour, because the lesson generalises.

The plan

Cheap, obvious plan: grab a spare Raspberry Pi, wire up an RC522 RFID reader (the ubiquitous blue board everyone uses for exactly this), and read/write fobs from a little script. I set the Pi up properly — Ansible to enable SPI, install the reader library, drop in a rfid command — held a fob to the antenna, and ran a read.

Nothing.

No error, no garbled data. Just silence, like there was no fob there at all.

Ruling things out

My first instinct was a wiring or hardware fault, so I went looking for evidence instead of guessing:

  • Wiring? I hammered the SPI bus with 3,000 reads of the reader’s version register and 2,000 write-and-read-back cycles. Zero errors. The connection was rock solid.
  • Dead reader? No — it happily read the sample card that came in the RC522 kit. The reader worked fine.
  • Weak field? I re-ran the scan at five different receiver gains, from maximum down to low. At every level: the kit’s card answered, the blue fob said nothing.

A reader that works, wiring that’s perfect, and a fob that’s simply not there as far as the radio is concerned. That’s not a bug. That’s physics.

Two radios that can’t hear each other

Here’s the thing nobody tells you when you buy an “RFID reader”: RFID isn’t one technology, it’s (at least) two, on two different frequencies that don’t interoperate at all.

Low frequency (LF) High frequency (HF)
Frequency 125 kHz 13.56 MHz
Common chips EM4100/TK4100, T5577 MIFARE Classic, NTAG, Ultralight
What’s on it a 40-bit ID, nothing more an ID plus writable memory (NDEF for phones)
Security none — the ID is broadcast in the clear can be encrypted (MIFARE keys)
Your phone (NFC) can’t see it reads and writes it

The RC522 is a 13.56 MHz reader. My blue fob is 125 kHz. They’re as mutually deaf as an AM radio tuned to an FM station. No amount of code, gain tweaking or antenna fiddling bridges that gap — it’s a hardware frequency mismatch.

The fob in question. It looks exactly like the 13.56 MHz MIFARE fobs in the RC522 kit — and is, in fact, 125 kHz. You cannot tell by looking.

And those cheap blue teardrop fobs? Almost always 125 kHz EM4100. They look identical to the 13.56 MHz MIFARE fobs that ship with the RC522 kit. Indistinguishable by eye, incompatible by radio.

The one-second field test: hold the tag to your phone with NFC on. If the phone reacts, it’s 13.56 MHz. If nothing happens, it’s probably 125 kHz. (My phone ignored the fob too — consistent with the diagnosis.)

Why I couldn’t just “add” a fob

The clean engineering answer to “I want more fobs” would be to enroll new ones: read each new fob’s ID and add it to the access controller’s allowlist. But I inherited this system — I don’t own the controller and can’t touch its config. So enrolling is out. The only route left is cloning: making a new fob that is byte-for-byte the old one.

For a plain 125 kHz EM4100 system, cloning is genuinely easy, because there’s nothing to crack — the fob just shouts a fixed 40-bit number, and that number is all the door checks. You copy it onto a T5577 blank, which can impersonate an EM4100, and the reader can’t tell the difference. (If the system were doing something cleverer — HID Prox, rolling codes — this wouldn’t work. But a cheap EM4100 setup almost never is.)

The actual tool

So, after all that: not the Pi. The right tool is a 125 kHz handheld copier — the little blue “RFID ID copier” with READ and WRITE buttons. It reads the original and writes a T5577 blank, standalone, no computer, ~€23 with a handful of blanks in the box. I ordered this Sotaiseo one from Amazon.de. Hold original → READ, hold blank → WRITE, test on the door. If the door opens, I can make as many as I like.

The €23 answer: a standalone 125 kHz handheld writer. Two buttons — READ and WRITE — and a pack of T5577 blanks. No computer required.

A €9 USB “reader” would have been a trap, by the way: it reads 125 kHz but can’t write, so it can’t produce a working copy. For cloning you need the writer.

The consolation prize

The Pi detour wasn’t wasted. It now has a tidy little rfid command and a small web UI (English + German, runs as a service, reads and writes from the browser) for 13.56 MHz chips — MIFARE and NTAG. Every write is verified by reading it back, and it refuses to touch the blocks that would brick a chip. Wrong band for my front door; exactly right for NFC stickers and the MIFARE cards I actually do have.

It’s one stdlib-only Python file plus an Ansible playbook, replacing the old Python 2 tutorials that don’t run on current Raspberry Pi OS. Code’s on GitHub: Marceltov/rfid-pi.

The takeaway

When something in the physical world refuses to work and your wiring and code are provably fine, stop poking the code and ask whether you’re even speaking the same language as the thing you’re talking to. “RFID reader” is about as specific as “wireless device.” Check the frequency first — it’s the one fact that decides whether the job is five minutes or impossible.

Next step: wait for the copier, confirm the fob really is the door key, and clone it. I’ll report back on whether the door agrees.

item.title: Lies of P: Overture – Wie ich den Tyrannischen Jäger nach 50 Versuchen geknackt habe
item.description: Der Tyrannische Jäger ist der erste große Boss im DLC Overture: ein mutiertes Krokodil im Savannen-Erlebniszentrum des Krat-Zoos. Schnell, unberechenbar, mit Schwanzschlägen nach fast jedem Angriff und einem …
item.content:encoded:
Der Tyrannische Jäger ist der erste große Boss im DLC Overture: ein mutiertes Krokodil im Savannen-Erlebniszentrum des Krat-Zoos. Schnell, unberechenbar, mit Schwanzschlägen nach fast jedem Angriff und einem Greifbiss, dessen Reichweite man ständig falsch einschätzt. Ein Gespenst kann man nicht rufen.

Nach rund 50 Versuchen hat es dann mit diesem Setup geklappt.

Die Waffe
Klinge Klinge eines Salamanderdolchs +10
Griff Griff eines Ehrenspeers
Klingen-Typ Dolch (Hieb und Stich)
Skalierung Technik A
Physischer ANG 106 + 49
Feuer-ANG 92
Gewicht 12,0
Schadensreduzierung beim Blocken 45,55 %
Fabel-Künste Entzünden, Rasender Schwung

Dazu das Amulett Arm Gottes: Es erhöht den Angriff, wenn man viele schnelle Treffer hintereinander landet.

Meine Werte

Attribut Wert
Vitalität 30
Stärke 20
Max. Ladung 35
Entschlossenheit 5
Technik 34
Fortschritt 6
LP 591
Ausdauer 161
Legion 283
Physische Verteidigung 187 (43,66 % Reduzierung)
Feuer-Widerstand 204

Der Trick: der aufgeladene Angriff

Das Wichtigste war, immer wieder den voll aufgeladenen Angriff zu nutzen. Mit dem Ehrenspeer-Griff kommt man dabei schnell hinter dem Krokodil her und macht viele kleine, schnelle Stiche hintereinander. Das hat drei Effekte auf einmal:

  • Er taumelt schnell. Die vielen Treffer bauen die Taumelleiste flott auf, und dann gibt es einen kräftigen Konterangriff.
  • Er fängt schnell Feuer. Jeder Treffer der Salamanderklinge baut Feuer auf, und der Jäger ist dafür sehr anfällig.
  • Arm Gottes zieht voll. Genau diese Serie aus schnellen Treffern ist es, wofür das Amulett den Angriff erhöht.

Was sonst geholfen hat

  • Den roten Ansturm nicht blocken, sondern seitlich wegsprinten und im letzten Moment rollen.
  • Bei Schnappangriffen auf den letzten Biss warten und erst dann zurückschlagen.
  • Immer an der Seite bleiben, nie direkt davor oder dahinter.
  • Nie in seiner Nähe heilen.
  • Traglast unter 80 % halten, damit das Ausweichen schnell bleibt.

Danach wartet hinter der Arena schon die nächste Überraschung, aber das ist eine andere Geschichte.

item.title: ELSTER: Behörden-IT, die einfach funktioniert
item.description: Bei Behörden-Software rechne ich mit dem Schlimmsten: Formulare, die mittendrin abbrechen, ein Ausweis, der irgendwie nur halb eingebunden ist, Fehlermeldungen, aus denen man nicht schlau wird. Nichts davon ist …
item.content:encoded:
Bei Behörden-Software rechne ich mit dem Schlimmsten: Formulare, die mittendrin abbrechen, ein Ausweis, der irgendwie nur halb eingebunden ist, Fehlermeldungen, aus denen man nicht schlau wird. Nichts davon ist passiert. Ich habe mich bei ELSTER registriert, dem Online-Finanzamt der deutschen Steuerverwaltung, danach den Login aufs Handy gelegt, und beides ging schneller, als ich dachte.

Warum ELSTER

Ich habe ein Gewerbe angemeldet: ein Einzelunternehmen unter meinem Namen, über das ich notefeed, Gamepanion und 3D Bruckner betreibe. Mit einem Gewerbe führt kein Weg am Finanzamt vorbei, und das Finanzamt ist online ELSTER. Also brauchte ich ein Konto.

Registrierung mit dem Online-Ausweis

ELSTER bietet fünf Wege zum Login. Für die Registrierung habe ich den Personalausweis genommen.

Fünf Wege zum Login. Ich habe den Personalausweis genommen.

Auf dem Mac läuft dafür die AusweisApp des Bundes. Bevor sie irgendwas vom Ausweis liest, zeigt sie, wer anfragt und welche Daten er bekommt: ELSTER, betrieben vom Bayerischen Landesamt für Steuern, und Name, Geburtsdatum, Anschrift, Dokumentart und ein Pseudonym. Das ist genau die Art Transparenz, die ich mir wünsche.

Die AusweisApp sagt vorher, wer welche Daten bekommt.

Ein Kartenlesegerät brauchte ich nicht: Das Handy ist der Kartenleser. Die AusweisApp auf dem Mac koppelt sich mit der AusweisApp auf dem Handy. Ich habe den Ausweis ans Handy gehalten, und nach dem Scan dort die sechsstellige Karten-PIN eingetippt. Das war’s.

Das Handy als Kartenleser: koppeln, Ausweis scannen, PIN eingeben.

Vom Klick auf „Login mit AusweisApp“ bis zum fertigen Konto vergingen ein paar Minuten. Nichts musste ich doppelt eingeben, und ich wusste immer, was als Nächstes kommt.

ElsterSecure: Login mit dem Handy

Danach habe ich ElsterSecure eingerichtet, die ELSTER-App fürs Handy, und das war ehrlich gesagt trivial. Seitdem zeigt ELSTER am Rechner einen QR-Code, ich scanne ihn mit der App, bestätige auf dem Handy und bin drin. Ohne Ausweis.

Login per QR-Code mit ElsterSecure. Den Code habe ich unkenntlich gemacht.

Jeder Login-Versuch gilt nur ein paar Minuten, die Uhrzeit steht direkt dabei. Ein abfotografierter Code ist danach wertlos.

Was nach dem ersten Login wartet

Gleich nach dem ersten Login weist ELSTER auf zwei Dinge hin, die ich richtig gut finde.

Die IBAN für Auszahlungen des Bundes. Der Staat kann bisher niemandem einfach Geld direkt überweisen; in der Corona-Krise oder bei der Energiepreispauschale ging das nur über Umwege. Jetzt gibt es dafür einen eigenen Zahlungsweg, gedacht etwa für das Klimageld. Das Bundeszentralamt für Steuern braucht dafür die IBAN, und die meldet man in Mein ELSTER mit einem einzigen Formular. Genutzt wird sie laut ELSTER nur für Auszahlungen.

Einmal die IBAN melden, damit der Bund direkt auszahlen kann.

Post vom Finanzamt digital. Ab 2027 darf das Finanzamt Bescheide und andere Schreiben direkt in Mein ELSTER bereitstellen statt per Brief. Wer weiter Briefe will, stellt das unter „Elektronische Bekanntgabe verwalten“ ein. Ich freue mich auf weniger Papier.

Ab 2027 kommen Bescheide in Mein ELSTER statt per Brief.

Kein Haken

Ich habe ehrlich gesucht und keinen gefunden. Der Ausweis ist sauber eingebunden, das Scannen klappt beim ersten Mal, jede Seite sagt genau das, was man gerade braucht. Das ist keine Selbstverständlichkeit, auch nicht bei Software von Firmen.

Danke an alle, die an ELSTER und der AusweisApp bauen. Wie war’s bei euch: Lief die Registrierung genauso glatt, oder seid ihr irgendwo hängen geblieben?

item.title: One repo, one home per fact: finishing the homelab consolidation
item.description: Today closed out a project that has been running for weeks: turning a pile of per-server repos into one repo for the whole homelab, and then deciding, once and for all, where each kind of documentation lives.
item.content:encoded:
Today closed out a project that has been running for weeks: turning a pile of per-server repos into one repo for the whole homelab, and then deciding, once and for all, where each kind of documentation lives.

From five repos to one

The homelab used to be spread over main-server, main-pbs, secondary-pbs-pi, proxmox and design. One by one they were folded in: both Proxmox hosts, the local Backup Server and the offsite Raspberry Pi backup box are now configured by Ansible from the same inventory. Today the last one went:

  • design, the shared PlantUML style for the architecture diagrams, stopped being a submodule. Its only other user had already been merged in, so it was pulled in with git subtree add (history kept) and the old repo archived. A fresh clone now renders diagrams without a submodule step, and a style change and its re-rendered SVGs are one commit.
  • The repo was renamed main-server → homelab. It had long stopped being about one server. GitHub renamed it in place, so issues, PR numbers and the 150 ADRs kept their numbers. Every URL in tracked files was rewritten; prose in old ADRs was left as written, because that is history. Nothing that runs depended on the checkout path — every unit, timer and backup hook is installed under /usr/local/lib/homelab/ — and that was checked on every host before the move.

That closes the central-repo programme.

One fact, one home

The bigger change was about documentation. The same machines were described in three places — the arc42 architecture doc, a Trilium wiki and Homelable — and they disagreed. Reading the live hosts against them found the architecture doc wrong about swap and kernels on both hypervisors, about how Frigate detects, how Jellyfin runs and which apps one guest hosts, and the wiki putting an app on the wrong guest.

The rule now:

Knowledge Lives in
Everything about one machine, runbooks Homelable
IP, MAC, CPU, RAM, disk Proxmox (shown in Homelable, never retyped)
Config, resources, firewall, backup jobs Ansible in the repo
Why something was decided an ADR
What went wrong a post-mortem
Architecture across machines arc42.md
General lessons and reading notes Trilium

Everything else links. ADRs and post-mortems stay in git on purpose: they merge in the same PR as the change they record.

What Homelable is

Homelable is a self-hosted, open-source app for documenting a homelab. It does three things that a wiki doesn’t:

  • It knows the devices. It imports machines from Proxmox and from its own network scan, so IP, MAC, CPU, RAM and disk come from the source rather than being typed in. A document is attached to a device, and Homelable marks it as drifted when the device’s facts change after the doc was written.
  • It draws them. Canvases are diagrams built from the same inventory: boxes are real devices, and a box can hold the containers running inside it.
  • It talks to Claude. It ships an MCP server, so a Claude session can search and read the docs, and write device docs, canvases and runbooks, the same way it reads a repo.

That last point is what tipped the decision: the docs are read by the same sessions that change the system, so they are worth keeping current.

How it is set up here

Homelable runs on its own small LXC container (CT 105, 2 GB RAM) on the main Proxmox host, deployed like every other guest: a git repo with one Docker Compose project and a deploy.sh, its secrets pulled from 1Password.

  • Three containers, from the upstream images: the web frontend (nginx), the backend (FastAPI, which also scans the network, hence the NET_RAW capability), and the MCP server.
  • All state is one SQLite file in a Docker volume: inventory, canvases and every document. The guest is in the nightly Proxmox backup, so that file goes through the full chain: local Backup Server, then the Raspberry Pi, then offsite. Its backup has been restored in a drill.
  • Access goes through the existing ingress. Caddy on the network guest publishes it on its own subdomain. Browser sign-in is OIDC against authentik, so it uses the same single sign-on as the rest of the homelab; the authentik provider is a blueprint in git. The MCP endpoint is reached through the same Caddy, with an API key instead of a login. One gotcha there: the MCP server answers /mcp with a redirect to /mcp/, and clients drop the API key on the redirect, so Caddy rewrites the path first.
  • A copy in git, for now by hand. A Sync button writes every document to a private GitHub repo, so the docs survive the host they describe. It has no schedule yet, which is why the restore runbooks still live in the architecture doc in the repo.
  • Monitored like everything else: the five fleet sidecars (logs, metrics, uptime monitor, image updates, dashboard discovery) run next to it.

The honest weak spot: Homelable runs on the host it documents. If that box is down, the docs about bringing it back are in the git copy and the architecture doc, not in the app.

What was built in Homelable

  • 26 device docs, one per machine, all in the same shape: purpose, why it is this way (each line linking its ADR), what runs here, what is special, where its operations differ, troubleshooting backed only by real incidents, dependencies, changelog.
  • 14 runbooks moved over from the wiki and corrected where they had gone stale.
  • A Services canvas: every guest with its running containers, checked one-to-one against docker ps, grouped into seven zones by function. Grouping by host was tried first and read as a pile, since 20 of 22 guests sit on one box.
  • A Backups canvas: 22 guests, which job backs each up and when, three tiers of storage — and, just as visibly, the eight guests that are deliberately not backed up.
  • The old hand-drawn network canvas was deleted; everything on it was already somewhere else.

On the Trilium side, 17 homelab pages were deleted once their content was confirmed in Homelable, and the rest trimmed down to the general lessons.

The lesson

Three copies of the truth don’t give you three times the safety — they give you three chances to be wrong, and no way to tell which one is. One home per fact, links everywhere else.

item.title: 3dbruckner.de sieht jetzt anders aus
item.description: Ich habe meine Seite neu gebaut. Der Grund ist einfach: Wer zu mir kommt, will sehen, was ich drucke, was es kostet und wie man bestellt. Die alte Seite hat zuerst viel erzählt und die Drucke erst danach gezeigt. Die …
item.content:encoded:
Ich habe meine Seite neu gebaut. Der Grund ist einfach: Wer zu mir kommt, will sehen, was ich drucke, was es kostet und wie man bestellt. Die alte Seite hat zuerst viel erzählt und die Drucke erst danach gezeigt. Die neue dreht das um.

Was neu ist

Die Fotos kommen zuerst. Auf der Startseite stehen acht Drucke mit einem ungefähren Preis. Im Portfolio findest du alle, sortierbar nach Kategorie.

Jeder Druck hat eine eigene Seite. Dort siehst du alle Fotos, den Richtpreis und einen Knopf „So etwas anfragen“. Das Formular weiß dann schon, welchen Druck du meinst.

Vier Wege zum Druck, gleich oben. Du hast eine Datei, einen Link, nur eine Idee, oder du willst erst den Preis wissen. Für jeden Fall gibt es einen direkten Einstieg.

Der Preisrechner gibt seine Zahlen weiter. Du trägst Gewicht und Druckzeit aus deinem Slicer ein und siehst sofort eine Schätzung. Mit einem Klick geht sie mit ins Anfrageformular.

Hell und dunkel. Die Seite folgt der Einstellung deines Geräts. Wer es anders will, schaltet oben zwischen Auto, Hell und Dunkel um.

Himbeerrot statt Orange

Die Farbe hat gewechselt. Das Logo ist geblieben, wie es war: das „3D“ mit der Maßlinie darunter, jetzt in Himbeerrot. Die Farbe steht auf der Seite nur noch dort, wo es ums Anfragen geht.

Was gleich bleibt

Der Ablauf ist derselbe: Du schickst mir eine Anfrage, ich melde mich innerhalb von 24 Stunden mit einem Angebot, und gedruckt wird erst, wenn du zugestimmt hast. Im Umkreis von etwa 10 km um Kempten bringe ich den Druck weiterhin persönlich vorbei.

Schau dich um: 3dbruckner.de. Wenn dir etwas auffällt, das hakt, schreib mir an kontakt@3dbruckner.de.

item.title: Redesigning this site: four directions, then a newspaper
item.description: This site has a new look since this week: a name across the top like a newspaper, serif text for reading, one colour per area, and a light and a dark version. This post is about how it got there, because the first …
item.content:encoded:
This site has a new look since this week: a name across the top like a newspaper, serif text for reading, one colour per area, and a light and a dark version. This post is about how it got there, because the first attempt was wrong in an instructive way.

What was wrong with the old one

Two things. The site looked like a template, and the blog looked like a changelog. Most posts were release notes of my projects, which arrive here automatically, and the few posts where I explain why I built something were buried between “0.31.1” and “0.32.0”.

The first attempt looked like my other site

I asked Claude for a redesign with the Open Design plugin, which produces mock-ups as plain HTML pages I can open on my phone. The first one was fine. It also looked very much like my 3D printing site, 3dbruckner.de, with different text.

That is what you get when you ask for “a redesign” without saying what the site is for. So I asked for several directions that differ on purpose, to have something to choose between.

  • Night signal (top left): dark and technical. I liked the mood.
  • Reading room (top right): the blog as the main thing. The right idea, but too quiet.
  • Allgäu (bottom left): mountains and warm colours. Too playful for me.
  • Index (bottom right): one big statement and a numbered list. The clearest of the four, and the best on a phone.

None of them was it, and each had one thing I wanted. So the next round mixed them, and one of the mixes had a centred name, a navigation line below it, one bold sentence and three coloured cards. That was the direction.

What the look is

  • Two typefaces with two jobs. A tight sans (Inter Tight) says what something is: statements, labels, numbers. A serif (Newsreader) tells the story: the name, the navigation, everything meant to be read.
  • One colour per area. Software is green, cloud is orange, 3D printing is pink, writing is blue. A colour only ever appears as a small square, a rule on top of a card, a number and an arrow.
  • Rules, not boxes. Sections are numbered and start with a line. Corners are sharp, and there are no shadows or gradients.
  • Light and dark. The site follows the device, and a switch at the top overrides it.

The switch remembers its setting in the browser’s local storage, not in a cookie, and the privacy page says so.

Essays first

The blog needed a rule more than a design. It is now this: a post tagged release is a release note, anything else is an essay. Essays get the page. Release notes sit in a side column, grouped by project, with the newest three each. The RSS feed carries essays only.

The posts still come from notefeed, one feed per topic, and the topic filter on the blog is simply the feed a post came from.

What the phone showed me

The mock-ups looked right. Then the real site was live and I opened it on my iPhone:

  • The arrow next to external links, a plain ↗ character, was drawn as a blue emoji. Text characters that have an emoji twin are not safe as icons. The site now uses real icons from Lucide.
  • The navigation wrapped so that one link sat alone on a second line. It is now a grid of three by two on small screens.
  • The order of the home page felt off: what I do, then numbers, then who I am, with parts repeating. “Who I am” moved up next to the opening statement, and the separate section went away.

None of this showed up in the mock-ups. I had looked at them, not used them.

Not one brand for everything

Halfway through I wondered whether this should become the look for everything I make: this site, the 3D printing site, notefeed, Gamepanion. It sounded tidy. I decided against it. A newspaper front page suits a site that is mostly writing. A shop needs its photos to carry the page, and a product needs to look like itself. So this look stays here, the 3D printing site gets its own design next, and the products keep theirs.

While I was at it

The content was as dated as the design. Several products were missing from the projects page, and the cloud page still described one server where there are two. The cloud page now follows the repository in which I keep that setup as code. There is also a new section for contributions to other people’s projects, and the text and my own pictures in these posts are now under CC BY 4.0.

The whole redesign was one long conversation, most of it spoken, and four pull requests.

item.title: passageway: Claude finds the right passage in your sources
item.description: Claude should find the right few passages in what you have written down, give you the links, and say nothing when nothing fits. passageway does that as a small server with one MCP tool, recall. It is the retrieval …
item.content:encoded:
The idea

Claude should find the right few passages in what you have written down, give you the links, and say nothing when nothing fits. passageway does that as a small server with one MCP tool, recall. It is the retrieval half of a RAG system. It never writes the answer itself: the model that calls it reads the passages and does that.

Why it exists

It grew out of trilium-recall, which does this for Trilium notes. The part worth keeping was never Trilium: it was the search, the relevance gate that keeps weak matches out of the prompt, and the habit of measuring. passageway pulls that out into a core that knows no source at all.

How it works

  • A connector is any program that lists items and prints their text as JSON Lines. It can be written in any language, and passageway ships a contract check that tells you whether yours is right.
  • The core indexes what connectors report, with keyword and embedding search in one SQLite file per source, on the CPU.
  • A relevance gate lets it return nothing instead of padding a prompt with a weak match.
  • Authentication is a bearer password, or an OAuth login page for remote clients.

What exists today (v0.1.0)

  • The core and the connector protocol
  • A Wikipedia connector that indexes a topic, some articles or a place, in English and German
  • A documentation site with a guide to writing your own connector
  • A release workflow that produced this feed: every tagged release posts its notes here

What comes next

A markdown connector and a frozen Wikipedia corpus, then an evaluation harness that measures retrieval quality on your own questions and builds a report you can publish. After that: a choice of embedding models, a container image, a Claude Code plugin for the prompt hook, and connectors for Trilium and Confluence.

Links

  • Documentation: https://passageway.marceltov.de/
  • Source: https://github.com/Marceltov/passageway (AGPL-3.0-or-later)
  • First release: https://github.com/Marceltov/passageway/releases/tag/v0.1.0

item.title: My Trilium setup: notes Claude can read, write and remember
item.description: My notes have lived in Trilium for years. Over the last few weeks they became something Claude works in too: it reads them before it answers, files what we figure out, and turns the articles I save into a wiki. This …
item.content:encoded:
My notes have lived in Trilium for years. Over the last few weeks they became something Claude works in too: it reads them before it answers, files what we figure out, and turns the articles I save into a wiki. This post is the map: which pieces there are, how they fit together, and where each one has its own post.

flowchart LR
  me["Me: browser, phone"] -- "save + tag" --> kk["Karakeep"]
  kk -- "tagged bookmarks" --> sync["karakeep-trilium-sync"]
  claude["Claude: Code, claude.ai, apps"] -- "MCP, OAuth login" --> proxy["trilium-mcp-proxy"]
  claude -- "recall" --> recall["trilium-recall"]
  subgraph T["Trilium"]
    mcp["built-in MCP server"]
    src["Sources"]
    wiki["Wiki"]
  end
  proxy --> mcp
  recall -. "reads" .-> T
  sync --> src
  mcp -- "ingest" --> wiki

The pieces

Piece What it does
Trilium 0.106+ The notes. Since 0.106 it has its own MCP server, so any MCP client can search, read and write them.
trilium-mcp-proxy Puts an OAuth login in front of that server: add one URL to claude.ai or Claude Code and log in with your Trilium password, no token to paste.
trilium-recall A search index next to Trilium (keywords plus embeddings, German and English) that hands Claude what the notes already know, before it starts guessing.
trilium-llm-wiki A Claude Code plugin that builds and maintains an LLM wiki inside Trilium, following Karpathy’s pattern.
trilium-plugin Claude Code skills for everyday notes: search, create, move, tag, templates, journal, export.
karakeep-trilium-sync Copies bookmarks I tag trilium in Karakeep into the wiki’s Sources every 15 minutes.

All of them are open source (AGPL-3.0-or-later) and run as small containers next to Trilium, or as plugins in Claude Code.

How knowledge gets in

  1. Collect. I save an article to Karakeep and tag it trilium. Reddit posts I save get the tag automatically.
  2. Sync. A few minutes later it is a read-only source note in Trilium.
  3. Ingest. I tell Claude “ingest”. It reads the source, writes a summary, updates the concept and entity pages it touches and logs the change in the day note. The rules for all of that live in a schema note in Trilium, so I change the wiki’s conventions by editing a note.
  4. Adopt. At the end of a work session Claude offers to file what we found: a decision, a fix, how a system actually behaves. Most of my wiki comes from this, not from articles.
  5. Review. Everything Claude writes is a draft marked AI-assisted until I set it to reviewed.

How it gets back out

Connecting Claude to Trilium isn’t enough: a model rarely stops to ask “do my notes know something about this?”. trilium-recall closes that gap. In Claude Code a prompt hook checks every prompt against the index and adds up to three short passages when the notes have something, and nothing when they don’t. On claude.ai the same engine is an MCP server whose instructions tell Claude when to look. In practice this is what makes the rest worth it: I speak a rough request (“the server from yesterday”, “like we did for the other repo”) and Claude starts from what I already wrote down.

What changed this week

  • Trilium’s own MCP server replaced mine. My ETAPI-based trilium-mcp is archived; the plugins now use the built-in tools, and trilium-mcp-proxy only adds the login.
  • trilium-recall became its own project, because it indexes all of Trilium, not only the wiki. Since 0.6.0 adding its URL to a client is the whole setup.
  • Release notes land here. Every release of these projects now posts its notes to this feed automatically.

Where to read more

  • trilium-recall: Claude remembers what you wrote in Trilium
  • An LLM wiki in Trilium
  • trilium-mcp-proxy: log in to Trilium’s MCP server with your password

Follow along with the RSS feed.

item.title: trilium-mcp-proxy: log in to Trilium's MCP server with your password
item.description: Since 0.106, Trilium has an MCP server built in, at /mcp. That's great news for anyone who uses Claude or another assistant with their notes: no more third-party server translating ETAPI into tools. It also meant the …
item.content:encoded:
Since 0.106, Trilium has an MCP server built in, at /mcp. That’s great news for anyone who uses Claude or another assistant with their notes: no more third-party server translating ETAPI into tools. It also meant the end of my own trilium-mcp, which did exactly that for two months and is archived now.

One thing was left: the login. Trilium’s MCP server takes an ETAPI token in the Authorization header. So for every client you create a token under Options → ETAPI, paste it into that client’s configuration, and remember where you put it. trilium-mcp-proxy removes that step.

What it does

You add the proxy’s URL to any MCP client (claude.ai, Claude Code, the Claude desktop and mobile apps) and log in once in the browser with your Trilium password. That’s it.

  • Your password stays on your server. The login page is the proxy’s own, next to Trilium. The password goes from your browser to it and on to Trilium’s /etapi/auth/login, which creates an ETAPI token for that client. The proxy never stores or logs the password, and the client only ever sees opaque OAuth tokens that work nowhere else.
  • Two-factor works. With TOTP switched on in Trilium, the login page asks for the code (since 0.1.1).
  • It’s transparent. Every /mcp request goes to Trilium unchanged, with only Authorization swapped. The tools are exactly Trilium’s, so new ones arrive with Trilium updates, without a proxy release.
  • House rules. Optionally, MCP_INSTRUCTIONS adds standing instructions to Trilium’s initialize answer, which every client reads when it connects. Mine says: there is an LLM wiki here, read its schema before writing, mark pages as AI-assisted, never write under Sources.
  • Revoking is simple. Each login is its own ETAPI token in Options → ETAPI. Delete it there, and that client is out.

Running it

Switch on Trilium’s MCP server (Options → AI / LLM → MCP server), then add one service next to Trilium:

  trilium-mcp-proxy:
    image: ghcr.io/marceltov/trilium-mcp-proxy:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      TRILIUM_SERVER_URL: http://trilium:8080
      MCP_BASE_URL: https://trilium-mcp-proxy.example.org   # public URL, behind your TLS proxy
      MCP_OAUTH_SECRET: ${MCP_OAUTH_SECRET}                 # openssl rand -hex 32
    volumes:
      - mcp-proxy-oauth:/data
    ports:
      - "8081:8081"

On claude.ai: Customize → Connectors → Add custom connector with https://trilium-mcp-proxy.example.org/mcp. In Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http trilium https://trilium-mcp-proxy.example.org/mcp -s user
# then /mcp → Authenticate

It uses about 20 MiB. I run one per Trilium instance (three in our household); I built a mode that serves several instances from one container and threw it away, because it saved little and tied all three to one secret and one failure point.

Gotchas with the built-in tools

Moving my plugins from trilium-mcp to Trilium’s own tools turned up a few differences worth knowing: they read and write Markdown, not HTML; set_attribute replaces an attribute of the same name; move_note on a cloned note moves only its original placement; and there is no tool for day notes, note maps or ZIP export yet. trilium-plugin and trilium-llm-wiki work around these.

The goal: retire it

The proxy is a stopgap. Trilium already has a login with password, TOTP and OpenID; it only needs to speak OAuth for MCP clients. I’ve proposed that upstream in TriliumNext/Trilium#12309: Trilium’s normal login plus a consent page, the access token being an ETAPI token named after the client, off by default, no schema change. If the maintainers agree, I’d like to build it, and then this proxy can go.

It’s licensed AGPL-3.0-or-later. Setup details are in the docs.

Discussion on GitHub: TriliumNext discussion #12310.

item.title: How freundebuch releases reach this feed
item.description: Until today freundebuch had no releases: every merge to main updated the :main image, and if you ran it you got whatever was newest. Now there are versioned releases, and each one shows up here on its own. The first, …
item.content:encoded:
Update, 13 November 2026: freundebuch no longer posts its releases to notefeed, and this feed has moved into my blog. The releases are on GitHub and on the projects page.

Until today freundebuch had no releases: every merge to main updated the :main image, and if you ran it you got whatever was newest. Now there are versioned releases, and each one shows up here on its own. The first, 0.1.0, is the note just below this one.

What happens on a release

I push a tag such as v0.2.0. GitHub Actions runs the same pipeline as on main: lint, typecheck, the unit tests, the Playwright tests and a smoke test that starts the container and waits for it to report healthy, while it builds the image for amd64 and arm64. Only when all of that passes:

  1. The image gets its version: ghcr.io/marceltov/freundebuch:0.2.0, :0.2 and :latest. A pre-release like v0.2.0-rc.1 only gets its own tag, so latest never points at one.
  2. A GitHub release is made, with GitHub’s generated list of the pull requests merged since the previous tag and a docker pull line.
  3. The same notes are posted here, tagged release and with the version, plus a link to the GitHub release.
flowchart LR
  T[tag v0.2.0] --> C[tests and smoke test]
  T --> B[image build, amd64 + arm64]
  C --> I[image tags 0.2.0, 0.2, latest]
  B --> I
  I --> R[GitHub release]
  R --> N[note on this feed]

For 0.1.0 the whole run took about 11 minutes from the tag to the note. A re-run doesn’t post twice: it first asks notefeed whether a note with that version tag is already there.

Pinning a version

To upgrade only when you choose, pin a version in your compose.yaml:

services:
  freundebuch:
    image: ghcr.io/marceltov/freundebuch:0.1

:main stays as it is, for everyone who wants every merge.

Good to know

The first release has no earlier tag to count from, so its notes list every pull request since the start (26 of them). From 0.2.0 on, each release lists only what’s new. The notes are PR titles, which are written for me more than for you; I’ll post a note in my own words alongside the bigger releases, like the two earlier ones on this feed.

The workflow is in .github/workflows/ci.yml. This feed has RSS at https://notefeed.me/r/freundebuch/feed.xml. If something about the release notes doesn’t work for you, tell me.

item.title: Roles, situations and a calendar feed
item.description: Over the last two days freundebuch learned the difference between who someone is to us and what's going on in their life. It also got a calendar feed, and Claude now gets told what to do after each call.
item.content:encoded:
Over the last two days freundebuch learned the difference between who someone is to us and what’s going on in their life. It also got a calendar feed, and Claude now gets told what to do after each call.

Roles are relationships now

“Our landlady” used to be filed as a fact, right next to the news about her new sink. Now it’s a relationship to the household: to “me” or to “us”. It’s written in plain German words for both ends (“Vermieterin” / “Mieter:in”) instead of a fixed type. People can have an optional gender, so the page reads “Unsere Vermieterin”. Claude only sets a gender when I say it or use a pronoun, never from the name. When a gender changes, Claude is told which words need regendering. That’s now only the neutral ones: setting 11 genders on my data listed 2 words to fix instead of 18.

Situations that nudge

Facts are split into two kinds. Gut zu wissen holds lasting ones (job, kids, allergies). Gerade los holds situations (a trip, a renovation). Each situation has a day to check in again. On that day it moves to the top of the page and into the daily push: “💬 Frag mal nach: Anna – sucht ein Auto”. Without a date it’s six weeks. When there’s news, Claude suggests a new day and agrees it with me before filing.

The person page also draws a small network: the household on top, the person in the middle, their people below, with a label on every line.

Tool results say what’s next

Every MCP tool result now carries next: short instructions built from what the call actually did. One example: “this situation nudges on 8 December, a default; tell the user.” Another: “two people match, ask which one.” Before, that guidance lived in the tool descriptions, where Claude had to remember it before it knew what the call had done. Now it arrives right after the call.

Also new

  • Calendar feed: birthdays (with the age when the year is known), other dates, and your own promises that have a due date, as an ICS URL you can subscribe to. Google refreshes it only every few hours, sometimes once a day.
  • Either of us can fix a shared item, not just whoever recorded it. Making an item private stays with the person who recorded it.
  • Softer background: slow colour bubbles that stand still if you’ve turned motion off.

Changelog on GitHub. Tell me what you’d want from the nudges.

item.description: You meet a friend and can't remember whether her new job has started, what her kid is called, or that you promised to send her a contact. I wanted something for that moment that doesn't ask me to fill in forms. So I …
item.content:encoded:
You meet a friend and can’t remember whether her new job has started, what her kid is called, or that you promised to send her a contact. I wanted something for that moment that doesn’t ask me to fill in forms. So I built freundebuch, a personal CRM for one household, where Claude does all the typing.

How it works

After a dinner I ramble about it to the Claude app, by voice or text. Claude files it through freundebuch’s built-in MCP endpoint: who was there, what’s new, what I promised, gift ideas, birthdays, who is related to whom. The full transcript is kept. Before I see someone again I ask “I’m seeing Anna tomorrow, what’s new?” and get a briefing: the last meetings, what’s going on, open promises, upcoming dates.

MCP is the main interface. Every feature works there first. A REST API (with OpenAPI) and a German web app sit on the same domain layer. The web app is mostly for looking things up on my phone:

  • The orbit: me in the middle, friends on rings by how long it’s been. Anyone overdue for their check-in interval drifts outward.
  • A page per person: what’s going on, what’s good to know, promises, dates, and the people around them.
  • Erzählen: a chat with Claude inside the app, using the same tools, for when I’m not in the Claude app.
  • Reminders once a day to a webhook such as ntfy: birthdays, promises, overdue friends.

Shared, with private parts

Two people in a household share one freundebuch. Anything said in confidence can be private to whoever recorded it, down to a single fact. Claude asks before filing when something sounds sensitive (health, money, relationship trouble). In the code, privacy is one function that every read goes through, so a private item can’t leak through a count or a summary. Tests check that by seeding a household.

What’s in it so far

I started on 23 October, and 44 PRs are merged as of today. Besides the core:

  • Groups with other names (“Kollegen” is “Arbeit”).
  • Screenshots from social media: share a friend’s Instagram or LinkedIn post and it lands on their page (“Urlaub in Lissabon · Instagram, 12. Oktober”). If Claude isn’t sure who it is, or it looks sensitive, it waits for me to check.
  • A calendar feed of birthdays and dates that Google Calendar can subscribe to.
  • Roles and situations: “our landlady” is a relationship to us, not a fact. “Renovating the bathroom” is a situation that nudges me to ask about it later.

What it isn’t

It isn’t a contact book (no phone numbers or addresses) and it isn’t multi-tenant: one instance per household, signed in through your own identity provider (authentik). It’s one container with one SQLite file, and it’s licensed AGPL-3.0.

The code is on GitHub, and the docs explain self-hosting. This feed is where I’ll post what changes. If you try it, I’d like to hear how the rambling feels.

item.title: An LLM wiki in Trilium: Claude builds and maintains a linked knowledge base
item.description: Andrej Karpathy described an "LLM wiki": you collect sources, and an LLM turns them into a wiki of linked pages, answers questions from it and keeps it tidy. People are good at choosing what to read and bad at the …
item.content:encoded:
Andrej Karpathy described an “LLM wiki”: you collect sources, and an LLM turns them into a wiki of linked pages, answers questions from it and keeps it tidy. People are good at choosing what to read and bad at the upkeep a wiki needs: cross-references, updating ten pages when one new source arrives, noticing contradictions. In this pattern, that upkeep becomes the assistant’s job.

Most setups build this on Obsidian and plain Markdown files. Trilium already has the pieces they build by hand, so I built mine on Trilium:

trilium-llm-wiki is a Claude Code plugin that builds and maintains an LLM wiki in your Trilium, using Trilium’s built-in MCP server.

Why Trilium fits so well

The pattern needs Trilium has
metadata on every page labels and promoted attributes, set by templates
a graph of linked pages internal links and relations, and the note map to look at it
pages of a few kinds templates (hub, concept, entity, source summary)
“what still needs work?” saved searches: pending sources, stubs, drafts, orphans
a log of what changed the journal’s day note
raw sources that stay untouched a #readOnly Sources subtree

How it works

  • One request sets it up: a Schema note, read-only Sources, the Wiki, four templates, saved-search views, two note maps and a lock folder.
  • The rules live in your Trilium: the schema note says how pages are written, linked and reviewed. Claude reads it before every write, and you change the wiki’s conventions by editing that note.
  • Workflows:
    • ingest a source: Claude writes a summary, updates the concept and entity pages it touches, creates placeholder pages for new topics, and logs the change in the day note;
    • query the wiki;
    • lint it;
    • adopt a finding from a work session.
  • You stay the editor: Claude writes drafts marked AI-assisted, and only you set a page to reviewed.
  • Safe with several sessions: a small write lock (a queue of claim notes) stops two Claude sessions from overwriting each other’s changes.

What goes in

  • Articles and links. I save them to Karakeep. A small sync job I wrote, karakeep-trilium-sync, puts them under Sources, and “ingest” does the rest.
  • My own chats with Claude. At the end of a session I just say “put this in the wiki”. Claude summarizes what we figured out or decided and files it into the pages it belongs to, so a fix, a decision or a “this is how it actually behaves” doesn’t get lost when the chat ends.

Finding things again

A wiki is only useful if the assistant actually looks things up. That’s what trilium-recall is for (my post about it): it gives Claude the relevant wiki pages before it answers, and the wiki’s structure helps it rank them, with wiki pages first and sources shown as their summaries. It works on any Trilium, so it has its own post.

Try it

You need Trilium 0.106+ with the MCP server switched on (Options → AI / LLM → MCP server). Connect it with an ETAPI token or through trilium-mcp-proxy (see discussion #12310).

/plugin marketplace add Marceltov/trilium-llm-wiki
/plugin install trilium-llm-wiki

Then ask Claude to “set up the LLM wiki”, drop an article under Sources and say “ingest”.

For everyday note work without a wiki (search, create, move, tag, journal, export) there’s trilium-plugin; both plugins share one connection.

Feedback is welcome, especially from anyone who runs something similar: how do you structure yours?

item.title: trilium-recall: Claude remembers what you wrote in Trilium
item.description: If you connect Claude (or any AI assistant) to Trilium, it can search your notes. But it rarely does that on its own. Before starting a task, a model doesn't stop to ask "do my notes already know something about …
item.content:encoded:
If you connect Claude (or any AI assistant) to Trilium, it can search your notes. But it rarely does that on its own. Before starting a task, a model doesn’t stop to ask “do my notes already know something about this?”, because it doesn’t know what it doesn’t know. So it works out again things you already wrote down, or gets them wrong.

trilium-recall fixes that. It’s a small container next to Trilium that indexes your notes and hands the assistant the few lines that matter. It runs as a plain MCP server, so any client can use it.

What it does

  • Indexes all your text and code notes, with keyword search plus a multilingual embedding model. It handles German and English, so a German note answers an English question. It only reads Trilium through ETAPI, and you can delete its index and rebuild it at any time.
  • Is just an MCP server. Add one URL to claude.ai, Claude Code or any other MCP client and you’re done: there’s no plugin and nothing to install on the client. The server’s instructions tell the model when to call recall. Each call returns up to three short passages with note IDs, or nothing.
  • Optional: runs automatically in Claude Code. A plugin adds a prompt hook that checks every prompt before Claude sees it. When your notes hold something relevant, Claude starts with it in the context. When they don’t, nothing is added.

In numbers

Measured on my own Trilium (280 notes, 49 test questions); yours will differ:

  • > 85 % of questions get the right note among the first three. Trilium’s built-in search manages around 40 %, because it needs every word of the question in the note.
  • > 90 % of questions the notes can’t answer get nothing back, instead of three weak guesses.
  • < 20 ms per lookup, typically.

Charts and the full comparison are on the Measurements page. The repo includes a public test Trilium, so anyone can reproduce the test numbers.

Running it

It’s one compose service next to Trilium, plus an ETAPI token and a password:

  trilium-recall:
    image: ghcr.io/marceltov/trilium-recall:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      RECALL_LOGIN_PASSWORD: ${RECALL_LOGIN_PASSWORD}   # openssl rand -hex 32
      RECALL_BASE_URL: https://recall.example.org       # public URL; turns on the OAuth login
      RECALL_INSTANCES: main
      TRILIUM_MAIN_URL: http://trilium:8080
      TRILIUM_MAIN_TOKEN: ${RECALL_ETAPI_TOKEN}
    volumes:
      - recall-index:/data
    ports:
      - "8082:8082"

Then add https://recall.example.org/mcp to your MCP client and log in once, or send the password as an Authorization: Bearer header. In Claude Code, for all your projects:

claude mcp add --transport http trilium-recall https://recall.example.org/mcp -s user
# then /mcp → Authenticate, and log in with RECALL_LOGIN_PASSWORD

On claude.ai, go to Customize → Connectors → Add custom connector and use the same URL. That’s the whole setup.

Optional: if you use Claude Code and want recall on every prompt, without the model deciding when to look:

/plugin marketplace add Marceltov/trilium-recall
/plugin install trilium-recall

Details: how it works, run the engine, connect Claude.

It started inside my LLM wiki and understands its structure when there is one, but it works on any Trilium. An embedding model inside Trilium itself seems unlikely given Trilium’s contribution rules (everything must work offline, and the bundle should stay small), so a separate container felt like the right place.

It’s licensed AGPL-3.0-or-later. Feedback is welcome, and I’d love to hear how it does on other people’s notes: the docs show how to measure your own.

item.title: Hello, blog: how this blog is made
item.description: For years my notes have lived in Trilium, and my projects in READMEs and docs sites. What was missing was a place to tell the story around them: why I built something, what I tried first, what broke. This post is …
item.content:encoded:
For years my notes have lived in Trilium, and my projects in READMEs and docs sites. What was missing was a place to tell the story around them: why I built something, what I tried first, what broke. This post is about how that place came about, on the same day as its first two posts.

Why a blog, and why like this

I didn’t want to write posts in an editor. I wanted to finish a piece of work and say to Claude: “write a blog post from this”. The conversation already holds the reasoning, the dead ends and the numbers; turning that into a post is exactly the kind of work an assistant does well. My part is the review.

I looked at a few setups:

  • Trilium as the CMS. My notes are already there, but the site’s build would need a Trilium token in GitHub’s secrets, and nothing in my Trilium is shared publicly on purpose.
  • Ghost. A good blog, but another server to run and update.
  • notefeed, the note feed service I build. A feed is a list of markdown notes with RSS, and anyone can read it through a public API without a key.

notefeed won. The blog is the feed notefeed.me/r/marcelbruckner, and this site shows it at /blog.

Talking, not typing

Most of what I say to Claude I say out loud. Speech input is fast, but it comes out half-formed: “the thing from yesterday”, “that server”, “like we did for the other repo”. That works because Claude doesn’t only get my words. It reads my second brain, my Trilium with its notes and an LLM wiki, and looks up what I mean: which server, which decision, what I tried last time. It is also connected to my GitHub, so it sees the repos, issues and pull requests I’m working on. A rough spoken sentence turns into a precise request, and a post like this one starts from everything that already happened instead of a blank page.

How a post gets here

flowchart LR
  I[Me: write a post from this] --> C[Claude writes a draft]
  C --> R{I review}
  R -- changes --> C
  R -- post it --> F[(notefeed feed)]
  F -- read API, no secret --> S[Site build]
  S --> B[marcelbruckner.de/blog]
  • Drafts first. Claude puts the draft in a separate drafts feed and shows me the whole text. Nothing reaches the blog until I say “post it”.
  • The site pulls the feed. An Astro loader reads the posts at build time and renders them with the site’s design, code highlighting and diagrams. A build that can’t reach notefeed fails, so a deploy never goes out without the posts.
  • Hourly rebuilds. The site checks the feed every hour and deploys only when something changed, so a new post shows up without a push. RSS works twice: on notefeed and at /blog/rss.xml.

The skills behind it

The workflow lives in two Claude Code skills. post-to-notefeed does the writing, the review and the posting for any notefeed feed, and anyone can use it: it ships with notefeed (Agent skills). A second, private skill adds what only this site needs: its tag rules (lang:de for German posts), the rebuild and the post’s address here.

What didn’t go smoothly

The first deploy failed. notefeed had just renamed a field in its API, and the site’s loader still asked for the old one. A one-line fix, but a good reminder that I am my own API’s first customer. Two things on notefeed’s side are still rough for long posts like this one: tags can’t be changed after posting yet, and notefeed’s own page doesn’t render diagrams. Both are open issues; on this site neither matters.

What comes next

Posts about what I build: AI tools around Trilium, self-hosting, my homelab, notefeed. The first two are about trilium-recall and an LLM wiki in Trilium. If you’d like to follow along, the RSS feed is the easiest way; feedback is welcome through the contact form.
